title: The folly of fully funding public schools.
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Victorian teacher Shaun Brien argues that fully funding government schools, while fair on equity grounds, will not solve problems if the money is spent poorly. Drawing on twelve years in the public system, he shows how funding is often used on expensive professional development that is one-and-done, on conference attendees expected to teach their colleagues, and on tokenistic tools for students with additional needs. He cites post-pandemic tutoring spending that pulled students from core instruction and school budgets going to visible aesthetics instead of dilapidated classrooms. He notes that no one is accountable for whether spending aligns with the state's explicit-teaching direction, so schools can pay for learning-styles talks or inquiry-focused training. His proposals are a school role that aligns spending and professional learning to shared priorities and a UK-style trust structure to share expertise. His conclusion is that what works in schools is inexpensive, but implementation is inefficient and needs more checks and balances.
points: More money does not guarantee better outcomes; Brien argues processes and priorities determine whether funding improves student learning.
Public schools often buy one-off consultant days or send staff to conferences, which leads to diluted or distorted implementation rather than lasting change.
Spending pressure can push special-needs budgets toward ineffective tools when time release for planning or hiring a literacy and numeracy expert would help more.
Limited accountability means a school can spend on debunked ideas like learning styles with no one questioning it.
He recommends a school-level role to align spending and PD with shared goals, and a trust-style network to share costly expertise.
quotes: I’m actually here to make the case that fully funding public schools is not the silver bullet it is made out to be
What is the point of funding if you can’t use it to improve student outcomes?
The government essentially threw money at a problem but did not look into the structure and processes important as to how that problem could be solved.
A big problem with school funding is that there is limited accountability on what schools spend their funding on.

This is an environment rife for lethal mutations as you are often relying on one or two teachers interpretations of a presenters summary of research where you are then likely going to find a school implementing a version of the strategy or practice which has morphed far from the original intention.
Too often, different silos within the school will run professional learning which is almost in direct opposition with the messages provided by the other.
What works is honestly inexpensive however implementation is currently inefficient.
